newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Coconut Oil - Prices seen softer in quiet market.
newsitem.headline: Coconut Oil - Prices seen softer in quiet market.

text.p: Coconut oil prices are expected to slightly soften this week due to prospects of more supply from the Philippines, Manila vegetable oil traders said on Monday.
"I expect the market to remain subdued this week as the big players are just emerging from the Christmas holidays," said one trader.

"Before the Christmas holidays, prices were high because buyers were aggressively buying coconut oil supposedly due to a dearth of copra from the Philippines. Now, it seems there is more copra and they are coming out from hiding," said another trader.
Prices softened after Christmas, they said.

Sellers quoted an average of $775.5 per tonne CIF of coconut oil in Europe the past week as against the previous week's $780.75, the trade group United Coconut Association of the Philippines Inc (UCAP) said.

State agency Philippine Coconut Authority last week said it expects the country's coconut crop to recover in 1997 after a sharp fall last year and its exports approach the all-time high of $1.1 billion.

PCA administrator Virgilio David forecast coconut production to reach 2.7 million tonnes this year. Production fell to an estimated 2.2 million tonnes in 1996 after it reached an all-time high of three million tonnes in 1995, he said.
David said the estimate of 2.2 million tonnes for 1996 was a revision of an earlier PCA forecast of 2.5 million tonnes.
A higher crop is expected this year because of a relatively good weather in 1996. Last year's coconut production was hurt by a series of typhoons that struck growing areas in late 1995, David said.
UCAP, however, forecast a lower 2.142 million tonnes this year from 1996's 1.966 million tonnes. The trade group also lowered its crop forecast in the past year from the earlier 2.334 million tonnes.

PCA's crop forecast was based on reports from coconut farmers about their expected harvests while the UCAP estimate was based on reports from both farmers and traders, which may account for the discrepancies in estimates.
UCAP also said it expected coconut exports in the first half of 1997 to be better while PCA said the bulk of exports would be in the second half of the year.

"Guaging from rainfall pattern this year, it is anticipated that export volumes during the first semester would be bigger, representing 53 percent of annual total, compared to the second semester," UCAP said.

David countered: "If UCAP said they expect exports in the first half to be better than the second half, then they may know something we don't know, like some traders or farmers may still be holding some stocks from last year and are waiting for better prices."
Traders said they were still trying to get actual numbers on the ending stock inventories in both Rotterdam and the United States in 1996.

Two boats, MV Blue Sapphire, with a cargo of 20,000 tonnes, is expected to arrive in Rotterdam between January 15 to 30, while the other boat MV Auriga, with a cargo of 16,000 tonnes, is scheduled to arrive in Europe later this month to early February.
